extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent drafters, patent attorneys, and IP professionals seeking guidance on drafting and assessing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether an invention is patentable and how to draft a patent application that satisfies core legal requirements across jurisdictions. Covers novelty, inventive step/nonobviousness, utility/industrial applicability, subject-matter eligibility, disclosure obligations, and related practical considerations (e.g., software, improvements, territoriality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability core requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable, an invention must fulfill several requirements, broadly classified as novelty, inventive step (nonobviousness) and industrial applicability (utility). Furthermore, an invention may be patented only if it is subject matter eligible for protection under the relevant national/regional law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary checklist for assessing patentability: (1) Is the subject matter eligible? (2) Is it novel? (3) Does it involve an inventive step / is it nonobvious? (4) Does it have industrial applicability / utility? If any of these fail, the invention is not patentable. Also ensure disclosure requirements (support, enablement, clarity, best mode where applicable) are met before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (no prior public disclosure / anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty generally requires that the claimed invention must not have been 'made available to the public' before the filing date (or priority date). The claimed invention is not novel if all of its elements are found in a single prior art reference (anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points and examples: a single reference must contain every claimed element to anticipate; examiners may not combine multiple references to destroy novelty (but can for obviousness). 'Made available to the public' includes oral disclosure, publications, use/display, exhibitions, social media. Use NDAs to preserve novelty when disclosing pre-filing. Jurisdictional notes: many countries treat worldwide disclosure as prior art; treatment of prior-filed but later-published patent applications (secret prior art) and grace periods varies by country (e.g., US/Japan have a one-year comprehensive grace period; Europe/China are more restrictive). Generic-versus-specific claims: a prior disclosure of a specific a1 can destroy a later generic claim A (if a1 ∈ A); the converse depends on distinguishing technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-filed, later-published patent applications (secret prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application filed in the same country before the filing (or priority) date but published only thereafter can become part of the prior art (secret or fictive prior art) in many jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictional differences: Europe and Japan typically use such prior-filed later-published applications for examining novelty only; the United States uses them for novelty and inventive step; in US and Japan a prior-filed later-published application is prior art only if filed by a third party (same applicant's earlier filings may be excluded), whereas Europe and China do not exclude same-applicant filings. Consider these rules when planning filing strategy and priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period / nonprejudicial disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions allow limited inventor/applicant disclosures within a defined grace period before filing to be non-prejudicial (not counted as prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and caution: the United States and Japan typically provide a one-year grace period covering any form of inventor disclosure; Europe and China are much more restrictive (exceptions such as disclosure at an international exhibition may apply). When seeking protection in multiple countries, file before any public disclosure whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / Nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must not have been obvious to a person skilled in the art. Nonobviousness means a person of ordinary skill could not have combined existing knowledge to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual differences from novelty: obviousness can be based on combining multiple prior art references. Typical analytical approaches: U.S. style — determine scope & content of prior art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, and the level of skill in the art; EPO problem–solution approach — identify closest prior art, establish distinguishing features, formulate the objective technical problem, and assess obviousness of the solution. Beware impermissible hindsight/ex post facto analysis. Consider 'teaching away' (if prior art discourages the claimed route, that supports nonobviousness) and secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others) as supporting evidence—though they rarely overcome a clear primary obviousness finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (hypothetical skilled practitioner)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothetical person (or team) skilled in the relevant art is assumed to have access to all publicly available prior art and ordinary practical skills, but not inventive capability beyond routine logic and experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The level of skill varies by field and may be a team of specialists for interdisciplinary inventions. This hypothetical standard is used to evaluate obviousness and enablement; do not conflate with a layperson or a leading specialist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible hindsight / Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examiners and courts must avoid hindsight (ex post facto) reasoning when assessing obviousness; conversely, a prior art reference that explicitly excludes or discourages an approach may 'teach away' and support nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if prior art states a particular component 'will not work', but the inventor nonetheless uses it successfully, that prior art may teach away. Avoid analyses that start from the invention and work backwards to prior art; instead, assess whether the skilled person, without knowledge of the invention, would have found it obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial application / Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be useful (utility) or capable of industrial application — i.e., it can be made or used in some industry (broadly construed) and achieves some minimally beneficial result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility generally requires only a practical, beneficial function – commercial viability is not required. Inventions contrary to well-established physical laws (e.g., perpetual motion machines) fail utility. In life sciences, laboratory effects (e.g., reducing tumors in lab animals) or usefulness as an intermediate may suffice. Professional tip: ask the inventor 'Are the results useful?' to screen for potential utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter / Subject-matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must fall within patent-eligible subject matter in the jurisdiction (e.g., US: process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter; Japan: creation of a technical idea utilizing a law of nature) and must not be an excluded category (laws of nature, abstract ideas, natural phenomena, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences by jurisdiction: some systems positively define eligible matter (US, Japan), others list nonpatentable categories (EPC). The EPC lists nonpatentable examples such as discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, aesthetic creations, schemes/rules for mental acts, business methods and computer programs 'as such', and presentations of information. Exclusion applies when claims are directed to such subject matter 'as such'; courts/boards test 'technical character' to distinguish eligible inventions. Field-specific examination guidelines may apply (software, business methods, biotech). Also note public-order/morality exclusions (ordre public), and special rules for diagnostic/therapeutic/surgical methods and plants/animals in some jurisdictions; products for use in medical methods may still be patentable. U.S. case law further refines exclusions (laws of nature, abstract ideas, natural phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software / computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Software-implemented inventions may be patentable if they produce a technical effect or implement a useful function in a new way; a pure mathematical algorithm or equation (mere software 'as such') is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual assumes software-implemented inventions can be patentable but warns that claims directed to pure mathematics are not. In jurisdictions following EPC practice, computer programs 'as such' are excluded unless they impart a 'technical character' or produce a technical effect. Draft claims to emphasize technical features and practical application to improve chances of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement patents and territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement patent covers an improved or enhanced effect compared with an earlier patent; however, practicing the improved invention may still require permission if it falls within the scope of earlier patent claims. Patents are territorial — protection applies only in the granting jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Inventor B obtains a patent for a faster filling machine with less spillage, but may need a license from Inventor A if A's claims cover B's embodiments. Licensing, cross-licensing and negotiation are common. Territorial implication: if Inventor A has rights only in Country X, Inventor B may practice the invention in other countries where A has no patent, subject to other patents in those countries. Consider patent mapping to identify blocking patents when planning exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement (public disclosure in exchange for exclusivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In return for exclusive rights, patent holders must sufficiently disclose technical information about the invention so that the public benefits and others can practice the invention after patent expiry. The disclosure requirement typically includes a support (written description) requirement, an enablement requirement, and a clarity requirement; some jurisdictions also require disclosure of the best mode known to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives: ensure the scope of claims is justified by the description/drawings and enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention. Practical consequences: you cannot add new subject matter after filing; inadequate disclosure can invalidate claims. Professional tip: assess disclosure carefully before filing to ensure claims are supported and enabling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement / Written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be supported by the description (support requirement), comparable to the United States' written description requirement: there must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and the claim scope must not exceed what is justified by the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is regarded as supported unless a person skilled in the art could not reasonably extend the particular teaching of the description to the whole field claimed. In the US, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that a person skilled in the art would reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at filing. Practical drafting guidance: disclose representative embodiments and variations, avoid overbroad claim language unsupported by examples, and plan for claim scope consistent with the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement, clarity, and best mode (components of disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement requires sufficient information for a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention; clarity requires that the claims and description clearly define the invention; best mode (in some jurisdictions) requires disclosing the best-known way of practicing the invention at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement and clarity are prerequisites to allow third parties to practice the invention and to delimit claim scope. Best mode is required in some countries (not universally) and failure to disclose it can be problematic in those jurisdictions. The manual points to later modules for practical drafting techniques to satisfy these requirements.
